slides.title: Twice the servers, no faster
slides.tldr: Add servers without measuring where it hurts and you spend money for nothing: the slow step is probably somewhere else.

blocks.title: The long line at the diner
blocks.body: At lunchtime the line outside a diner stretches down the street, so the owner hires 5 more waiters, going from 5 to 10. The line doesn't shrink at all. Everyone is stuck at the single cash counter, where one person writes up every bill.

Tyler's shop app went through the same thing. On sale day the site crawled, so the team doubled the app servers from 4 to 8, yet checkout still took 3 seconds. The time was going into one slow database query. The step that holds everybody up is called the **bottleneck**, after the narrow neck of a bottle.

blocks.caption: Where the 3 seconds of checkout actually went

items.label: Network and nginx
items.tip: The time for the request to reach the server and for the reply to travel back. Nothing to win here.

items.label: PHP code
items.tip: The app server's own work. Doubling servers only helped this part, which is just 5% of the total time.

items.label: Database query
items.tip: This is the cash counter. Without an index, one query was scanning the whole table; 85% of the time goes right here.

items.label: Payment API
items.tip: Waiting for an outside service to answer. No matter how many servers you add, this time won't shrink.

blocks.body: Measure first, then scale. Pouring power into a step that isn't stuck buys you nothing.

aside.body: When a site is slow, the first reflex is "give it more servers". This step teaches which numbers to measure so you can tell where it is really stuck, and put your effort in the right place.

items.meaning: The slowest step. It decides the speed of the whole system.
Increasing a system's capacity so it can handle more load.

items: Adding app servers while the database is the stuck part means more connections and more queries hitting it. Things get worse, not better.

items.label: The fix for this exact query

check.q: Why didn't doubling the waiters shorten the restaurant's line?
check.a: Because everyone was stuck at the cash counter, not at the waiters. Speeding up anything other than the slowest step (the bottleneck) doesn't make the whole thing faster.

slides.title: Three numbers: load, throughput, latency
slides.tldr: Load is how many requests arrive, throughput is how many get finished, latency is how long one takes. Near capacity, latency shoots up.

blocks.title: Counting at the restaurant door
blocks.body: Count how many people walk into the restaurant each minute: that's the **load**. Count how many finish eating, pay and walk out each minute: that's the **throughput**. The time one person spends from entering to leaving is the **latency**. If the cash counter can't handle more than 10 people a minute, then even with 12 arriving per minute only 10 leave. The rest pile up in the line, and everyone's wait keeps growing.

blocks.caption: The three numbers, in the restaurant and in the app

rows.tip: The pressure comes from outside, and you don't control it. On a Black Friday sale the load can jump tenfold by itself.
The work the system is actually getting done. It has a ceiling, and that ceiling is called capacity.

cells: Time to get the reply to one request
rows.tip: Waiting in line plus the real work, added together. This is the only number the user ever feels.

blocks.caption: The busier the server, the more latency jumps (each job takes 10ms, so one worker tops out at 100 requests/s)

items.label: 50% busy
items.tip: The server is idle half the time, so almost nobody has to wait in line.

items.label: 80% busy
items.tip: The work itself is still 10ms, but waiting in line makes the total five times that.

items.label: 90% busy
items.tip: Just 10% more load and latency doubled. This is where the trouble starts.

items.label: 95% busy
items.tip: Another 5% and it doubles again. At 100% the line never empties.

blocks.body: A worker that needs 10ms per request can finish at most 100 a second. At 50 a second the line is nearly empty. At 90 a second the same worker answers in 100ms, ten times the work itself. So if your busiest moment brings 700 requests a second, plan capacity for about 1,000, not 700. The price is paying for 30% idle capacity, and that idle part is what keeps the wait short.
Never plan to keep a server 100% busy. Past 70-80% the line builds up and latency jumps.

aside.body: Load goes in, throughput comes out, latency is the wait in between.

items.meaning: Requests (or queries) per second, the unit for measuring load and throughput.
The maximum throughput the system can deliver.
The percentage of its capacity that a resource is busy.

items.label: What to do when load exceeds capacity

check.q: Load is rising, throughput is stuck at one value and latency keeps growing. What does that mean?
check.a: The system has hit its capacity. The extra requests aren't being finished, they're piling up in line, so everyone's wait grows.

slides.title: Averages lie: p50, p95, p99
slides.tldr: The average hides the slow requests. p95 and p99 show how long your worst-served users are waiting.

blocks.title: 95 happy, 5 furious
blocks.body: Out of 100 customers at the restaurant, 95 got their food in 10 minutes and 5 got it an hour later. The average works out to 12.5 minutes, which sounds fine, yet 5 people stormed out angry. So sort everyone by wait time. **p50** means half the customers were served faster than this, **p95** means 95 out of 100, and **p99** means 99 out of 100. That slow stretch at the end is called **tail latency**.

blocks.caption: The same checkout endpoint over the last hour: average vs percentiles

items.label: p50 (median)
items.tip: Half of all requests finished faster than this. It is the experience of a "typical" user.

items.label: Average
items.tip: A few very slow requests dragged the average up. Almost nobody actually got an answer in this time, so the number is nobody's real experience.

items.label: p95
items.tip: One request in every 20 is slower than this. An SLO (the target you promise, like "p95 under 300ms") is usually written in terms of this number.

items.label: p99
items.tip: One request in every 100 takes more than 4 seconds. You would never spot this by looking at the average.

blocks.body: p99 sounds rare, but it isn't. If building one page takes 20 internal calls, about 18% of pages, roughly 1 in every 5 or 6 users, include at least one call as slow as the p99.

blocks.code:
SELECT
    round(avg(duration_ms))                                    AS avg_ms,
    percentile_cont(0.50) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms)  AS p50,
    percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms)  AS p95,
    percentile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms)  AS p99
FROM request_log
WHERE route = 'checkout'
  AND created_at > now() - interval '1 hour';

marks.tip: The average is only here for comparison. Base your decisions on the three percentile lines below it.
Sorts all rows by duration_ms and picks the value at the 99% position. That is p99.
Measure each endpoint separately. Mix every route together and a slow endpoint disappears among the fast ones.

blocks.body: Don't measure latency with averages. p50 shows the typical experience, p99 the worst. Look at both.

items.meaning: The middle value: half the requests are faster, half slower.
Faster than 99% of requests; the other 1% are slower still.
The latency of the few slowest requests (p99, p99.9).

items: Write goals as percentiles: "checkout p95 under 300ms". "Fast on average" is not a goal.
You can't add up or average the p99s of separate servers. Merge their histograms first, then compute.
Your biggest shoppers send the most requests, so they are the ones who land in the tail most often.

items.label: Metrics, SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

check.q: Why is it wrong to look at an average latency of 310ms and say "all good"?
check.a: The average hides slow requests behind the fast ones. Here p99 is over 4 seconds: 1 request in 100 is very slow, and the average gives you no way to see it.

slides.title: Little's Law: how many are inside at once?
slides.tldr: Requests in flight = requests arriving per second × average latency. This one multiplication sizes your workers and connections.

blocks.title: How many chairs do you need?
blocks.body: Two people walk into the restaurant each minute, and each stays 30 minutes on average. So at any moment 2 × 30 = 60 people are inside, and you need 60 chairs. If a slow kitchen stretches each stay to 60 minutes, the same customers need 120 chairs. That multiplication is **Little's Law**: L = λ × W.

blocks.caption: The same sum for an app: how many PHP-FPM workers do you need?

steps.title: 1. Measure load (λ)
steps.body: At the busiest time, 200 requests arrive per second.
steps.tip: λ (lambda) is the arrival rate. Take the peak figure from the nginx access log or your metrics, not the all-day average.

steps.title: 2. Measure average latency (W)
steps.body: One request takes 0.25 seconds on average.
steps.tip: W is how long a request stays inside the system on average. This formula needs the average, not a percentile.

steps.title: 3. Multiply (L)
steps.body: 200 × 0.25 = 50 requests in flight at once.
steps.tip: L is the number of requests inside at the same moment. In PHP-FPM every running request occupies one worker, so you need at least 50 workers.

steps.title: 4. Add headroom
steps.body: Add 20% spare: max_children = 60.
steps.tip: You need some idle workers to absorb sudden bursts. But check that it fits in RAM: 60 × 60MB ≈ 3.6GB.

steps.title: 5. Think of a slow day
steps.body: If W becomes 1 second, L = 200: four times the workers.
steps.tip: The load didn't grow at all, only the database got slow, yet every worker gets stuck and new requests join the queue. More workers is no cure (200 × 60MB = 12GB of RAM). Cut W: fix the slow query, or set a database timeout.

blocks.code:
; L = 200 req/s x 0.25s = 50 requests in flight  ->  keep 20% spare, so 60
; static keeps all 60 workers in RAM (60 x 60MB = 3.6GB), even at 3am
pm = static
pm.max_children = 60

; the page that shows "active processes" and "listen queue"
pm.status_path = /fpm-status

; a stuck request must not hold a worker forever
request_terminate_timeout = 30s

marks.tip: At most 60 requests run at once. Request number 61 waits in line (the listen queue).
If the listen queue stays above zero, either workers are too few or latency has grown.

aside.body: How many are inside = how fast they arrive × how long they stay.

items.meaning: How many requests arrive per second.
How long a request stays in the system on average, including time waiting in line.
The average number of requests inside the system at the same moment.

items: The same formula sizes a database connection pool, a queue worker fleet, even the headcount of a call center.
Before adding workers, see whether you can cut W. Halve the latency and you need half the workers.

check.q: 100 requests arrive per second and the average latency is 0.5 seconds. How many requests are in flight at once?
check.a: 100 × 0.5 = 50. So you need at least 50 workers, plus some spare. If latency grows to 1 second, you need 100.

slides.title: Find the bottleneck before you scale
slides.tldr: Measure how much time each step of a request takes. Fix the step that takes the longest or fills up first.

blocks.body: The restaurant owner only needed to look at where the line was forming. In an app, measurement does that looking for you: write down the time of each step of a slow request, and see how full each resource is.

blocks.title: Four steps to find it
items: Pick the slow endpoint by its p95/p99, not by a hunch.
Split its time: PHP code, database queries, outside APIs, waiting in line.
For each resource check three things: how busy it is, whether a queue is building, whether errors appear.
Fix the biggest slice, then measure again. The bottleneck will move somewhere else.

marks.tip: Symfony's Stopwatch component, which autowires in. In dev these steps also show up in the Profiler's Performance tab.
stop() returns an event; getDuration() gives the time in milliseconds. A separate number per step shows who is guilty.
In production the numbers go to a structured log. From there you can compute p95/p99 per step.

blocks.caption: What it looks like when each resource fills up, and where to look

cells: 90%+ busy, load average above core count
rows.tip: This is the only case where adding app servers directly helps.
All workers busy doesn't mean the CPU is short. Most of the time they are sitting and waiting on a slow database or API.
Once connections run out, new requests can't even reach the database. Adding app servers makes this run out faster.

cells: some queries run for seconds on end
rows.tip: This is where most CRUD app bottlenecks are found: a missing index, or N+1 queries.
More servers won't fix this. You need timeouts, a cache, or to move the work to a queue.

items.desc: where the query really spends its time

items.cmd: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
items.desc: how many database connections are busy, how many idle
active workers and the listen queue

items: Don't make production decisions from measurements on your laptop. On a table of 100 rows every query is fast.
Change five things at once and you won't know which one helped. Change one, then measure.

items.label: Next: the index fix, before and after
Indexes and reading a query plan

check.q: Of checkout's 3 seconds, 2.5 go into one query. What happens if you double the app servers?
check.a: Latency stays about the same, and the database gets more pressure. Fix the query first (an index, a smaller query), then measure again to find the next bottleneck.

slides.title: The fix: an index, before and after
slides.tldr: A missing index made one query read 4 million rows. Add it and that step drops from 2,550ms to about 1ms, checkout from 3,000ms to about 450ms, and the next bottleneck shows itself.

blocks.body: Back to Tyler's checkout. The slow step looked up one product among 4 million rows. With no index on `sku` (the product code), the database read every row to find it, like reading a whole phone book to find one name. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows that, and an index (the phone book's alphabetical order) fixes it.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT quantity FROM stock_items WHERE sku = 'BR-500';

-- before: no index on sku
Seq Scan on stock_items  (rows=1)
  Filter: (sku = 'BR-500'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 3999999
Execution Time: 2548.220 ms

-- after: index on sku
Index Scan using idx_stock_items_sku on stock_items  (rows=1)
  Index Cond: (sku = 'BR-500'::text)
Execution Time: 0.041 ms

marks.tip: It read and threw away 3,999,999 rows to keep one. This is where the 2.5 seconds go.
Index Scan: it jumps straight to the row, like opening the phone book at the right letter.
CONCURRENTLY builds the index without blocking writes on the live table. The price: it is slower to build, and it can't run inside a transaction.
The price of any index: more disk, and a little extra work on every INSERT and UPDATE of stock_items. Index the columns your slow queries filter on, not all of them.

blocks.caption: Checkout after the index: about 450ms instead of 3,000ms, and the payment API is now the biggest slice

items.label: Network and nginx
items.tip: Unchanged. The request still has to travel.

items.label: PHP code
items.tip: Unchanged. Twice the app servers never touched the real problem.

items.label: Database query
items.tip: From 2,550ms to about 1ms: the same query, now an index lookup instead of reading every row.

items.label: Payment API
items.tip: Now the biggest slice, over half of the 450ms. This is the next bottleneck, and an index can't help an outside service.

items: An index doesn't cure every slow query. If EXPLAIN already shows Index Scan and it is still slow, the query returns too many rows or joins too much.
Running plain CREATE INDEX on a busy table blocks its writes while it builds. Use CONCURRENTLY.

items.label: Indexes and reading a query plan

check.q: After the index, checkout takes about 450ms. What do you look at next, and why?
check.a: The payment API: 250ms, over half of the total now. The bottleneck moved, so measure again. An index can't help it; a short timeout, or moving work around it into a queue, might.

slides.title: One upload form, and the whole shop is gone
slides.tldr: When the app, the database, the photos and the backups share one server and one disk, a single hole reaches all of them, and a single runaway job fills the disk under all of them.

blocks.body: Nicole's shop, Green Basket, runs on one VPS with a 100 GB disk. On it live the Symfony app, MySQL (12 GB), 60 GB of product photos and seven nightly backups of 3 GB each. The system takes 4 GB and 3 GB is free. The photo form saves each file under the name the visitor sent, inside `public/uploads/`, and nginx runs any `.php` file it finds there.

blocks.caption: One uploaded file, and every part on the box is reached

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: Needs no password. The upload form is open to every visitor, because customers send photos with it.

nodes.label: Upload form
nodes.tip: The folder is served by nginx and anything ending in .php gets executed. This is the hole.

nodes.label: .env file
nodes.tip: The app must be able to read this file, so a script running as the app can read it too.

nodes.label: MySQL
nodes.tip: Listens on the same machine, so the password from .env works straight away. Nothing else stands in the way.

nodes.label: Backups
nodes.tip: Seven dumps of 3 GB each, in a folder the app's user can write to. Whoever controls the app can delete them.

edges.label: The attacker uploads shell.php as a "photo" and opens its URL
The script runs as the app's user and reads the database password from .env
With that password it dumps every customer and order
It deletes the seven backups too, because they sit on the same disk

blocks.body: On another night nothing is stolen at all. A bot posts 3 GB of images, the free space is gone, and MySQL cannot write any more, so every order fails. Same box, same disk, same story: one thing goes wrong and everything goes with it.

items.meaning: The folder the web server hands out directly to visitors. Here that is `public/`.
A tiny script an attacker uploads that lets them run commands on your server from a browser.
A virtual private server: one rented machine, usually with one disk.

aside.body: The pieces on this box have very different jobs, but they share a door (the web server), a password file, a CPU and a disk. When one piece is hurt, the others have no wall to hide behind.

check.q: In the story, the hole was an upload form. Which two other facts about the box turned that one hole into three losses?
check.a: The database password sat in `.env`, readable by the app, and the backups were on the same disk in a folder the app could write to. All of it was reachable from one machine.

slides.title: Blast radius: split what must not fail together
slides.tldr: Blast radius is how much one break-in or one runaway job can reach. Split the box so each part gets its own machine, its own door and its own failure.

blocks.title: One drawer, or a register, a back room and a storage unit
blocks.body: Picture a corner store that keeps the cash, the house tab book (the notebook of who owes what), the stock and the spare copy of the tab book in one drawer behind one lock. One stolen key or one fire takes the lot. Now split it: the register stays at the front, the tab book goes to a locked back room that only the cashier may enter, the stock goes to a storage unit across town, and the spare tab book goes home with the owner. Each one now needs its own break-in.

blocks.title: What a single box shares
items: One door: a break-in through the web app reaches the database, the photos and the backups.
One CPU and RAM: a heavy report query slows every web request.
One calendar: you cannot patch or scale the database without touching the app, nor the other way around.
One disk: when it fills or dies, the data, the photos and the backups go together.

blocks.caption: After the split, every part has its own place, and the attacker's way in is shut

nodes.label: Customers
nodes.tip: Real shoppers. They only ever talk to the load balancer.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: Tries the database directly, as any scanner on the internet would.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.tip: The only part with a public address. It spreads requests over the app servers.

nodes.label: App tier
nodes.tip: The Symfony app, in copies that keep nothing inside themselves, so any one can be replaced or patched while the others work.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.tip: On its own host or a managed service. It has a private address, and only the app tier may connect.

nodes.label: Object storage
nodes.tip: Product photos live here, not on any server's disk. Nothing uploaded here is ever run as code.

nodes.label: Backups
nodes.tip: Copies kept away from the machines they protect, so what hurts one does not hurt the other.

edges.label: A customer's request reaches the load balancer
The load balancer hands it to one of the app servers
The app asks the database over the private network only
Photos are written to object storage, not to the app's disk
Backups are copied to a separate place, away from the database host
The attacker tries the database directly: refused, it has no public address

blocks.body: Whatever shares a machine, a disk or a password can fail, or be broken into, together.

items.meaning: How much of the system one failure or one break-in can damage.
Several locks in a row, each assuming the one before it has failed.
The group of identical app servers that run your Symfony code and keep no state of their own.

items.label: Load balancers and single points of failure

check.q: A heavy monthly report makes the shop's pages slow. Which shared thing is hurting, and what does the split change?
check.a: CPU and RAM are shared. With the database on its own host, the report no longer steals the web server's CPU and RAM. Sending reports to a replica protects the database as well.

slides.title: Make the database listen on the private network only
slides.tldr: Bind the database to its private address and let in only the app subnet: bind-address for MySQL, listen_addresses plus one pg_hba.conf line for PostgreSQL.

blocks.body: Moving the database to its own host is only half the job. If it still listens on every address, any scanner on the internet can try passwords against it. Tell it to listen on the private address only, and keep the database port closed in the firewall as a second lock. MySQL first: the red line is the lazy fix that "makes it connect from anywhere".

blocks.code:
[mysqld]
-bind-address = 0.0.0.0     # every network card, the public one too
+bind-address = 10.0.1.5    # only this host's private address
 port         = 3306

marks.tip: 0.0.0.0 means "all addresses of this machine". With a public address on the machine, the whole internet can reach port 3306.
Listens only on the private address. Machines outside the private network cannot even open a connection.

blocks.body: PostgreSQL uses two files. `listen_addresses` chooses the addresses it listens on, and `pg_hba.conf` chooses who may log in from where. The single `host` line below lets one user into one database, and only from the app subnet. A managed database offers the same two locks as "not publicly accessible" plus a security group, as in [[infra/cloud-primitives/open-door-database|private subnets and security groups]].

blocks.code:
# postgresql.conf
listen_addresses = 'localhost,10.0.1.5'   # never '*' on a database host

# pg_hba.conf
# TYPE  DATABASE  USER      ADDRESS      METHOD
host    shop      shop_app  10.0.1.0/24  scram-sha-256

marks.tip: Localhost for admin work on the host itself, plus the one private address. Nothing public.
Read it as: the user shop_app may reach database shop from 10.0.1.0/24 with a hashed password. Every other address is refused.

blocks.body: A database gets a private address and a short list of who may call it.

items.desc: on the database host: it must show 10.0.1.5, not 0.0.0.0
from your laptop: it must fail

items: Do both: bind to the private address and close the port in the firewall. If one is changed by mistake, the other still holds.
The price: the app and the database now talk over a network, so a wrong firewall rule or subnet breaks the shop. Test the connection after every change.

check.q: Why is `bind-address = 0.0.0.0` dangerous even when the database password is strong?
check.a: It makes the database reachable from every network the machine is on, the internet included. Bots can then try passwords and known bugs. Listen on the private address and allow only the app subnet.

slides.title: Give the app a database user that can do very little
slides.tldr: The running app needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on its tables, and nothing else. Give it exactly that, keep a separate user for migrations, and point DATABASE_URL at the private host.

blocks.body: Today the app logs in as `root`, so a web shell inherits root and can `DROP` every table. Create one user for the running app with only the rights the code uses. A second user, used only during deploys, may change the schema.

blocks.file: run once as an admin on the database host

marks.tip: Exactly what the code does at runtime. No DROP, ALTER or CREATE, no other database, and no global rights such as FILE.
Only the deploy pipeline holds this user. A script that gets into the running app never sees its password.

blocks.code:
# the running app: the limited user, on the private host
DATABASE_URL="mysql://shop_app:CHANGE_ME_app@10.0.1.5:3306/shop?serverVersion=8.0"

marks.tip: The host is the database's private address, and the user is shop_app. The migrate user's URL stays in the deploy pipeline and is never put on the app servers.

blocks.body: The deploy step runs `DATABASE_URL="$MIGRATE_DATABASE_URL" php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction`. Be honest about the limit: a script inside the app can still read and change rows, because the app can. Least privilege shrinks the damage, it does not remove it.
Each layer assumes the one before it has already failed.

items: PostgreSQL: `GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO shop_app`, plus `USAGE` on the sequences so inserts get their ids.
Doctrine's Messenger transport can create its own table at runtime. Set `auto_setup=0` and run `messenger:setup-transports` in the deploy step.
The price: two users and two passwords to store and rotate, and a migration run with the wrong URL fails. That failure is the point.

items.desc: see exactly what the app user may do

items.meaning: Every user and program gets only the rights it needs for its job, and no more.

check.q: A web shell now runs inside the app, and the app uses `shop_app`. Name one thing it can still do and one thing it no longer can.
check.a: It can still read and change rows, as the app does. It can no longer `DROP` or `ALTER` tables, create new users, or touch other databases.

slides.title: Uploads and backups: the cheap basics, even on one box
slides.tldr: Before you split anything: never let the web server run files from the uploads folder, validate and rename every upload, and push backups to a place the server cannot delete from.

blocks.body: These steps cost almost nothing and cut the exact chain from the story. In the diff, the red block is the generic PHP handler that runs any `.php` file, `shell.php` in `uploads/` included. The green blocks pin `/uploads/` so nothing in it is ever run, and hand only `index.php` to PHP, as Symfony's own nginx recipe does.

marks.tip: Any URL ending in .php is passed to PHP-FPM, so /uploads/shell.php runs as code. This is how the attacker got in.
^~ makes this prefix win over the regex rules, and inside it every .php request is refused.
Only the front controller, index.php, may be executed. Every other .php file gets a 404.

blocks.title: And on every upload
items: Store files outside `public/` (for example `var/uploads/`) and serve them through a controller, or use object storage.
Check the real type and size on the server (`#[Assert\Image]`, `client_max_body_size`), not in the browser.
Ignore the visitor's file name: save as a random name such as `Uuid::v7()` plus an extension you chose.
Keep uploads on their own volume or under a quota, so a flood fills that, not the disk MySQL writes to.

blocks.body: Backups need the same care. A dump on the same disk dies with the disk and with the intruder. Copy it to another place, and use a key that can add files but not delete them. More in [[recovery/backups-restore/backup-that-never-restored|backups and the 3-2-1 rule]].

blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

f="/var/backups/shop-$(date +%F).sql.gz"
mysqldump --defaults-extra-file=/root/.backup.cnf --single-transaction shop | gzip > "$f"

# 'backup-writer' may only add objects (s3:PutObject), it cannot delete old copies
aws s3 cp "$f" "s3://shop-backups-offsite/db/" --profile backup-writer

rm -f "$f"    # nothing is left on this disk for an intruder to find

marks.tip: The copy goes to a bucket outside this server. Switch on bucket versioning or Object Lock too, so even an overwritten file can be recovered.
The local copy is removed, so the box never holds the only or the latest backup.

items: Validation can be fooled. Treat it as a second lock, and treat object storage as the real fix, because nothing there can ever run.
A backup key that can also delete lets an intruder wipe the remote copies as well.

check.q: Why is a nightly dump kept in a folder on the same server not a real backup?
check.a: The same break-in, disk failure or mistaken `rm -rf` that hits the database hits the dump too. Copy it to another place with a key that cannot delete.

slides.title: What the split costs, and when one box is fine
slides.tldr: The split adds a network hop to every query, more parts to run and a bigger bill. A single box is still fine for a prototype or a tiny internal tool, if the cheap basics are in place.

blocks.body: Nothing here is free. Every query now crosses a network, typically about 1 ms inside one data center, against well under 0.1 ms to a database on the same box. One query will not notice. A page that runs 200 queries, the N+1 problem where a list triggers one extra query per row, now waits 200 ms longer. The fix is to load those rows in one query with a JOIN.

blocks.caption: Extra waiting added by the network, at about 1 ms per query

items.label: 1 query
items.tip: A single lookup. You will never notice the hop.

items.label: 20 queries
items.tip: A normal page with a few lists. Still hardly visible.

items.label: 200 queries (N+1)
items.tip: One extra query per row of a list. On one box this hid in the noise, across a network it is a fifth of a second.

items.label: 200 rows, one JOIN
items.tip: The same page after loading the rows in a single query. The hop is paid once.

blocks.caption: One box against the split, and what each costs

cells: A break-in through the web app
rows.tip: The attacker must break into each part separately, and each part has its own credentials.
The database still feels the report. Run reports on a replica to protect it too.
You can patch the database at night and add app servers at noon, without touching the other.
Photos in object storage and backups elsewhere do not share the database disk.
The price in latency. Harmless for one query, visible for hundreds.
More to monitor and patch, and a new failure: the network between the tiers can drop or slow down.
A load balancer, extra app servers and a managed database each add their own line to the bill.

blocks.title: One box is fine for a prototype, with the basics kept
items: The database listens on localhost or a private address, never on a public one.
Uploads cannot run scripts, and the app has a least-privilege database user.
Backups are pushed off the box with a key that cannot delete.
The firewall opens only 80, 443 and SSH.

use: The shop takes real orders and a lost day of data would hurt
Reports or imports slow down the web pages
The app and the database need different patch or scaling schedules
avoid: A prototype or a tiny internal tool: one box plus the basics is fine
You have not measured the bottleneck yet: find it first

check.q: After moving the database to its own host, a list page with 200 queries feels slower. What happened, and what is the best fix?
check.a: Each query now pays about 1 ms of network time, so 200 queries add about 200 ms. Load the rows in one query with a JOIN instead of one query per row.

slides.title: One big server, or many small ones?
slides.tldr: Vertical means making one server stronger, horizontal means adding more identical servers. The first is easy but has a ceiling; the second has none, but your app must be ready for it.

blocks.title: The crowd at the pizza place
blocks.body: When the crowd grows, the owner has two options. One: buy a bigger oven, so it's still a single shop. Two: open a second location down the street. A big oven has a limit, and on the day you repair it the whole shop is closed. With locations the crowd gets split, and if one shuts the other keeps serving.

blocks.caption: Two answers to the same crowd

columns.title: Vertical (scale up)
items: No code changes
A little downtime while you switch
No way forward past the biggest machine
If the machine dies, everything is down
columns.tip: One machine, just more CPU and RAM. You don't touch the code, so for a first attempt it is the cheapest option.

columns.title: Horizontal (scale out)
items: Add small servers to add capacity
If one dies, the rest keep working
You need a load balancer to split the crowd
The app must be stateless
columns.tip: Many copies of the same app run side by side. Capacity is almost unlimited, but the app has to be prepared for it in advance.

blocks.body: Vertical is easy but has a ceiling. Horizontal has no ceiling, but your app has to be ready for it.

use: Vertical: you need relief right now and the server is small
Horizontal: the site must stay up even if a server dies
avoid: Vertical: the database is already on the biggest machine
Horizontal: the app still keeps things in its own server's files

items.meaning: Putting more CPU, RAM and disk into the same machine.
Adding more machines to do the same job.

check.q: Your goal is for the site to stay up even if a server dies. Vertical or horizontal, and why?
check.a: Horizontal. With many servers, the rest carry on when one dies. If your one big server dies, the whole site is down.

slides.title: The rule for many servers: nobody remembers anything
slides.tldr: To run the app on many servers, no server may keep sessions, files or cache inside itself. That data lives in Redis, the database and object storage.

blocks.title: Switch locations, where is the house tab?
blocks.body: If every location kept its own house tab book, where the shop writes down who owes what, Kevin could run up a tab at location 1 and walk into location 2 as a stranger. So all locations read one central tab book. Servers work the same way: a user's login, cart and uploaded photos can't live on one server's own disk or in its memory.

blocks.caption: The same user, two servers, one Redis

nodes.label: Kevin
nodes.tip: The same Kevin sends two requests. He doesn't know which server each one lands on, and he doesn't need to.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.tip: Sends each request to a different server. Nothing in the app may depend on which request goes where.

nodes.label: App server 1
nodes.tip: One copy of the app. If it dies or a new copy joins, nothing is lost.

nodes.label: App server 2
nodes.tip: Exactly the same code and behavior. It never has to talk to the first server.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.tip: The central tab book everyone shares. Both servers read Kevin's session from here.

edges.label: Kevin's first request arrives and he logs in
The first request goes to server 1
Server 1 writes Kevin's session to Redis
This time the request goes to server 2
Server 2 finds the session in Redis, so Kevin stays logged in

blocks.title: What must never live inside a server
items: Sessions (login state): they belong in Redis or the database
Uploaded files: they belong in object storage (S3-compatible)
In-memory cache that others need to know about: it belongs in Redis
A cron or scheduler that would run twice, once per server: run it in just one place

aside.body: Once something piles up inside a server, that server becomes "special". Special servers are hard to delete or copy, so horizontal scaling gets stuck.
Servers are cattle, not pets: lose any one and nobody notices.

check.q: A user logs in, but the next request lands on another server and asks them to log in again. Why?
check.a: The session was stored in the first server's own file or memory. Move sessions to one place everyone shares (Redis or the database).

slides.title: Move sessions and files out in Symfony
slides.tldr: Switch the session handler to Redis and write uploads to object storage instead of local disk. Two small changes make the app horizontal-ready.

blocks.body: Symfony's default session is stored as a file on the server's disk, and uploads usually go to `public/uploads`. Both work fine on one server and break on two. Start with the session: put a Redis DSN in `handler_id` and Symfony sets up the RedisSessionHandler for you.

blocks.code:
framework:
    session:
        # .env: REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/1
        handler_id: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'
        cookie_secure: auto
        cookie_samesite: lax
        gc_maxlifetime: 1800     # session expires after 30 idle minutes

marks.tip: Give it a DSN and Symfony uses the RedisSessionHandler. From now on every app server reads sessions from the same place.
The session TTL in Redis comes from this value, so old sessions delete themselves.

blocks.body: Now uploads. Declare the storage once in `config/packages/flysystem.yaml` (a storage named `uploads.storage`, with the `aws` adapter and your bucket). In the diff below, the red line stores the file on this server's disk, where no other server will ever see it. The green lines write to object storage through Flysystem, which looks the same to every server.

marks.tip: move() puts the file on this server's disk. If the load balancer sends the next request to another server, the photo returns a 404.
writeStream() sends the file to object storage as a stream, so even a big file never has to be loaded into memory whole.

items: Store the object storage URL in the database, not a path on the server.
If you lose the Redis sessions, users just log in again. So keep nothing critical in a session; critical data goes in the database.
The price: every request now makes one Redis call, and if Redis is down nobody can log in. Give it a replica or use a managed Redis with failover.

items.desc: see which session handler is active
check that session keys are landing in Redis

check.q: Before running the app on two servers, which two places must you change in Symfony at minimum?
check.a: The session handler (Redis or the database) and file uploads (object storage). Both are currently stored on the server's disk, which other servers can't see.

slides.title: Autoscaling wakes up late
slides.tldr: Autoscaling adds servers when it sees load, but measuring, deciding, starting and health checks take a few minutes. A sudden spike breaks the servers during exactly that time.

blocks.title: The extra cooks at a wedding
blocks.body: When more guests show up than expected, the manager phones for extra cooks. They have to arrive, wash their hands and get the stoves going, and that takes a long while. Meanwhile the guests stand in line. An autoscaler is the same: it sees the crowd and makes the call, but a new server takes time to become useful.

blocks.caption: After the crowd arrives, a new server takes 270 seconds in total to start working

items.label: Metrics collected
items.tip: CPU numbers are usually collected once a minute. Even if the crowd is already here, the autoscaler knows nothing for the first minute.

items.label: Decision to scale up
items.tip: The autoscaler looks at an average and doesn't move on a single spike. This wait keeps a false alarm from adding servers.

items.label: Server starts, image pulled
items.tip: Getting a new machine or pod, pulling the container image and starting PHP. This is the slowest step.

items.label: App warm-up
items.tip: A new app starts cold: the Symfony cache isn't warm and opcache isn't filled. The first requests are slow.

items.label: Health check passes
items.tip: The load balancer confirms the server is healthy, and only then starts sending it requests.

marks.tip: The most useful line. Keep 6 servers running before the crowd arrives and you skip the 270-second wait.
Scaling up starts once CPU passes 60%. If you wait for 80-90%, latency has already spiked before the new server arrives.
Waits 5 minutes before scaling down. Otherwise servers get cut the moment the crowd thins, and you suffer when the next wave comes.

blocks.body: Autoscaling wakes up late. For known crowds (Black Friday, sales), scale up in advance.

items: Without a max, a buggy loop or an attack can grow your servers and your bill without limit.
Without a readiness check, a new pod receives requests while it is still cold.
minReplicas costs money around the clock. For a one-night sale, raise it an hour before and lower it after.

items.meaning: One running copy of your app in Kubernetes. More pods means more servers doing the same job.
The Kubernetes autoscaler. It watches CPU and adds or removes pods.

aside.body: Autoscaling handles slow waves, not sudden jumps. For jumps you need servers added in advance, plus a rate limit.

items.label: Holding off overload until new servers arrive

check.q: A flash sale starts at exactly 8 pm, and the crowd jumps 10x at that moment. What happens if you rely on autoscaling alone?
check.a: For about 4-5 minutes the old servers have to absorb the crowd, and latency and errors rise. Raise the minimum count before the sale starts.

slides.title: Scale the database last
slides.tldr: App servers are easy to add, the database is not. More servers mean more database connections and load, so fix queries, add a cache and replicas first, and shard last.

blocks.title: The locations multiply, but the warehouse stays one
blocks.body: The pizza chain goes from 4 locations to 20, but they all fetch their flour and cheese from the same central warehouse. Now people from 20 locations are jostling at its door. Adding app servers does exactly this: everyone's pressure lands on a single database.

Do the math: 20 app servers with 25 PHP-FPM workers each, one connection per worker, makes 500 connections. If Postgres has `max_connections` at 200, the new servers can't even get into the database. The fix is a connection pooler, such as PgBouncer, which lends real connections out one transaction at a time. It has limits; the next slide shows them.

blocks.code:
[databases]
shop = host=10.0.0.5 port=5432 dbname=shop

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction       ; connection goes back when the transaction ends
max_client_conn = 1000        ; connections coming in from the apps
default_pool_size = 20        ; only 20 real connections to the database

marks.tip: It doesn't hold a connection for every query; it hands the connection to someone else as soon as the transaction ends. So few connections serve many clients.
1000 clients, but the database sees only 20. Each transaction holds a connection for a few milliseconds, so 20 real ones serve 500 workers in turns, like 20 registers serving a long queue.

blocks.caption: When the database is slow, work through these in order

steps.title: 1. Fix the queries
steps.body: Add indexes, remove N+1
steps.tip: The cheapest and most rewarding step. Many apps get 10 times faster right here.

steps.title: 2. Add a cache
steps.body: Put data read again and again in Redis
steps.tip: It cuts the number of requests that reach the database at all, so the database gets room to breathe.

steps.title: 3. Read replicas
steps.body: Reads can come from a replica
steps.tip: Writes stay on the primary, and the read load gets shared. You do have to keep replication lag in mind.

steps.title: 4. A bigger machine (vertical)
steps.body: A more powerful database server
steps.tip: For databases, vertical is often the simplest option. Using it up to its limit is perfectly fine.

steps.title: 5. Shard
steps.body: Split the data across many databases
steps.tip: The most powerful and the most expensive. Cross-shard queries and transactions get hard.

items.meaning: One PHP process that handles one request at a time. 25 workers means 25 requests in parallel.
A middleman that holds a few real database connections and lends them to many clients.
Loading a list with one query, then one more query for every row of it.

aside.body: Before you add pressure on the database, cut the database's work.

check.q: After going from 4 to 20 app servers, the database throws "too many connections". What is the first fix?
check.a: Put a pooler like PgBouncer in front, so the database holds only a few real connections. Just raising max_connections eats the database's RAM.

slides.title: PgBouncer transaction mode: what it breaks
slides.tldr: Transaction pooling lends a connection for one transaction only. Prepared statements, SET, advisory locks and LISTEN/NOTIFY assume the same connection stays yours, and break. Fix: emulate prepares, go direct for the rest.

blocks.title: Twenty registers, five hundred shoppers
blocks.body: A shopper writes a note and leaves it at register 7, expecting to find it there next time. But the shop sends every visit to whichever register is free, so the note is at register 7 while the shopper stands at register 12. Transaction pooling works like this: anything you leave on "your" connection is gone by your next transaction.

The classic PHP victim is the prepared statement. PDO prepares the query on one connection, then runs it on another, and Postgres answers `SQLSTATE[26000]: prepared statement "pdo_stmt_00000001" does not exist`. Tell PDO to send plain queries instead; the values are still escaped.

blocks.code:
doctrine:
    dbal:
        # DATABASE_URL points at PgBouncer, port 6432
        url: '%env(resolve:DATABASE_URL)%'
        options:
            !php/const PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES: true   # no server-side prepares

marks.tip: PDO builds the SQL itself and sends it in one go, so nothing is left on a connection that the next transaction would lose. PgBouncer 1.21+ can instead track prepares if you set max_prepared_statements.

blocks.code:
# migrations (and LISTEN/NOTIFY, advisory locks) go straight to Postgres, port 5432
DATABASE_URL='postgresql://app:CHANGE_ME@10.0.0.5:5432/shop?serverVersion=16' \
    php bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate --no-interaction

marks.tip: Only this command gets the direct URL. The running app keeps using PgBouncer.

blocks.title: Also lost in transaction mode
items: `SET search_path` or `SET timezone`: lost, or leaks to another client. Use `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction.
Session-level advisory locks, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, temporary tables: go direct.

use: Many app servers: total workers are far above `max_connections`
avoid: Few servers whose workers already fit in `max_connections`: no pooler needed
Code that leans on session state: use session mode or a direct connection

items: PgBouncer is one more process in front of the database. Run two, or it becomes the next single point of failure.

check.q: After switching to PgBouncer in transaction mode, some queries fail with "prepared statement does not exist". Why, and what is the fix?
check.a: PDO prepares on one pooled connection and executes on another. Turn on PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES (or PgBouncer 1.21+ max_prepared_statements).

slides.title: When one box dies, everyone dies
slides.tldr: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any part that stops the whole system when it dies. Two app servers aren't enough: the load balancer can be a SPOF too, and a standby twin fixes it.

blocks.title: The bus station with one ticket counter
blocks.body: The bus station has 10 buses but only one ticket counter. If the clerk steps out for a break or falls ill, nobody can buy a ticket, even though the buses are right there. The buses are your app servers and the counter is the load balancer. Adding more buses doesn't fix the problem.

blocks.caption: What happens when each part of Tyler's shop dies

rows.tip: There are several copies, so when one dies another keeps working. That is redundancy.
Every request passes through it, yet there is only one copy. This is the biggest mistake.
Even with replicas, when the primary dies writes stay down until a new primary is chosen. You need failover.

cells: A power cut takes everything down
rows.tip: If servers, LB and database all sit in one place, one incident takes them all. You need multiple availability zones.

blocks.body: Ask every box: what happens when you die? If the answer is "everything stops", that box is a SPOF.

aside.title: Two servers, still down
aside.body: A small online shop figured that two app servers made it safe. One night the disk on its only nginx server filled up. Both app servers were healthy, yet the site was down for 40 minutes.

items: Run two load balancers. When one dies, the other takes over the same IP (the next slide shows how), or use your cloud's managed LB.
When you draw a new system, write "how many copies?" next to every box.

check.q: With two app servers and one nginx, which one is the SPOF, and how do you remove it?
check.a: The nginx. Make it two as well, using a floating IP like keepalived, or use a cloud managed load balancer, which already runs in several places.

slides.title: A standby twin that takes over the IP
slides.tldr: Run two load balancers that share one IP. The active one holds it and sends heartbeats; if they stop, the standby claims the IP within seconds. keepalived does this with VRRP.

blocks.body: Give the two load balancers one shared address, a **virtual IP**, and point DNS at it. LB A holds it and sends a heartbeat every second over **VRRP**, a tiny "I'm alive" message. If LB B hears nothing for about 3 seconds, B claims the IP and visitors never notice the address changed.

blocks.caption: LB A crashes at 2am: the same address keeps working

actors.label: Visitor
actors.tip: Knows only one address, 203.0.113.10. Never learns which box answers.

actors.label: LB A (active)
actors.tip: Holds the virtual IP and sends a heartbeat every second.

actors.label: LB B (standby)
actors.tip: Does no work, only listens for A's heartbeat.

messages.label: Request to 203.0.113.10
messages.tip: In normal times every request lands on A.

messages.label: Heartbeat: I'm alive
messages.tip: Sent once a second. B stays quiet as long as these keep coming.

messages.note: 3 seconds of silence: B claims the IP

messages.label: Retry to the same 203.0.113.10
messages.tip: The address is unchanged; it simply points at B now.

marks.tip: Without this check, a box whose nginx died but whose machine is alive would keep the IP and drop every request.
When the higher-priority box dies, the lower one wins. When it returns, it takes the IP back.

blocks.title: What it costs, and when it fails
items: The standby sits idle, so you pay for a second box and get no extra capacity.
Requests in flight when A dies are lost; only new ones succeed, after about 3 seconds.
If the link between A and B breaks but both live, both claim the IP (split brain).

use: Your own servers or VMs in one network, where you control the IPs
avoid: Most clouds block VRRP; use the provider's managed load balancer instead
You need more capacity, not just survival: that needs several active LBs

items.meaning: An address that belongs to no single machine; whoever is active holds it.
The protocol where boxes in a pair keep telling each other "I'm alive".
Both boxes think they are the active one and both claim the IP.

check.q: LB A's machine is up but its nginx has crashed. Which line of the config makes B take over?
check.a: The `track_script` that runs pgrep nginx. After 2 failed checks A gives up the IP and B claims it.

slides.title: Three rules for splitting the crowd
slides.tldr: Round robin takes turns, least connections picks whoever has the least work, weighted gives bigger machines more. The best choice depends on how uneven your requests are.

blocks.title: Seating guests among the wedding waiters
blocks.body: When a new guest arrives, which waiter's table does the manager pick? **Round robin**: 1, 2, 3, taking turns. **Least connections**: whoever has the fewest tables right now. **Weighted**: three tables for the most experienced waiter, one for the newcomer. If all tables are alike, taking turns is enough. If some tables sit all night, you have to keep count.

blocks.caption: The three rules compared

rows.tip: The simplest, and the default. It counts requests but doesn't look at how heavy each one was.

cells: Requests are tiny and the bookkeeping costs more
rows.tip: It counts open connections, so a slow server automatically receives fewer requests.

cells: A wrong weight drowns one server
rows.tip: A weight is really a capacity ratio. Some people combine it with round robin or least connections.

blocks.caption: Six requests, three servers; every third one is a 30-second report

columns.title: Round robin
items: Turns go A, B, C, A, B, C
Both 30s reports land on A
A is busy for a minute; B and C idle
columns.tip: Takes turns blindly. The heavy requests are 1 and 4, and turn 4 lands on server A again.

columns.title: Least connections
items: Report 1 goes to A
Report 4 sees A busy and goes to B
Each server holds one report
columns.tip: Asks who is least busy right now. When report 4 arrives, A is already holding one, so it goes elsewhere.

blocks.title: A simple way to choose
items: With no particular reason, start with round robin.
Some requests run for seconds (uploads, exports)? Choose least connections.
Servers unequal? Set weights.

aside.body: Equal work: take turns. Uneven work: pick the least busy. Uneven machines: use weights.

items.meaning: The servers behind nginx that requests are sent to.
How many times more requests one server gets compared to another.

check.q: Some requests run for 20 seconds, the rest finish in 10ms. Which rule makes it less likely that one server piles up, and why?
check.a: Least connections. Round robin hands the same number to a server stuck with slow requests, while least connections skips the busy server and sends work to an idle one.

slides.title: nginx upstream and health checks
slides.tldr: Write the rule, weights, failure limits and a backup server in an nginx upstream. Add a cheap /healthz that an active checker (HAProxy, a cloud LB) calls; free nginx only checks passively.

blocks.body: A load balancer takes just a few lines of config. Here `max_fails` and `fail_timeout` give you a **passive health check**: when real requests fail, nginx sidelines the server for a while. Poking the server ahead of time, an **active health check**, isn't in free nginx. That is what the `/healthz` endpoint below is for: HAProxy (`option httpchk GET /healthz`), nginx Plus or a cloud LB calls it every few seconds.

marks.tip: After 3 failures the server is skipped for 10 seconds. weight=3 means it gets three times as many requests as the small server.
The backup server gets no requests in normal times. It steps in only when all the others are down.
When one server fails, nginx retries the same request on another. By default it does not do this for POST, so an order isn't placed twice.
When the drain file exists it returns 503, so the LB stops sending new requests. Requests already running get time to finish.
If the database had a small hiccup, this check would fail on every server at once and the LB would pull them all out. A minor problem becomes a full outage.

items: If the health check calls the database or an outside API, the moment that gets slow every server turns "sick" at once and the whole site goes down.
Free nginx never calls /healthz and never reads the drain file; it only reacts to real failures. Pair it with an active checker for drains.
Behind a proxy, set `framework.trusted_proxies` in Symfony, or the user's IP will always show up as the LB's IP.

check.q: What does max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s mean in nginx?
check.a: If real requests fail 3 times within 10 seconds, the server is skipped for the next 10 seconds. After that nginx tries it again.

slides.title: L4 vs L7: the address on the envelope, or the letter inside?
slides.tldr: An L4 load balancer looks only at IP and port and forwards TCP: fast, and works with any protocol. L7 reads HTTP, so it can decide by path, header and cookie.

blocks.title: Two kinds of post office worker
blocks.body: One worker looks only at the address on the envelope and drops it in a sack. They never learn what's inside, so they're very fast. The other opens and reads the letter, and if it's "urgent" puts it in a separate sack: more work, but smarter. The first is **L4**, the second **L7**.

blocks.caption: At which layer the crowd gets split

columns.title: L4 (TCP)
items: Any TCP: PostgreSQL, Redis, MQTT
Very fast, low CPU
Doesn't understand paths or cookies
TLS usually gets opened on the servers behind it
columns.tip: Looks only at IP and port and passes the connection along. It never reads the message inside, so it is very fast.

columns.title: L7 (HTTP)
items: /api to one group, /images to another
Opens TLS right here (termination)
Retries, rate limits, adding headers
Only for HTTP/gRPC
columns.tip: It opens up the HTTP, so it can decide by path, header and cookie. It does need more CPU.

marks.tip: nginx reads the URL of the HTTP request, so /api and /images can go to different servers.
In a stream block nginx is just a pipe of bytes and doesn't understand the database protocol. Even so, reads can be spread across replicas.

use: L7: web apps, APIs, routing by path or host, TLS in one place
L4: databases, Redis, games or any other non-HTTP protocol
avoid: L7: for a protocol that isn't HTTP
L4: when you must split by path or cookie

items.meaning: The reliable pipe that most programs use to send bytes to each other, web or database.
Opening the HTTPS encryption at the load balancer, so the servers behind it receive plain HTTP.

check.q: On one domain, /api should run on 3 servers and /admin on a separate one. L4 or L7?
check.a: L7. To see the path you have to open and read the HTTP request, and L4 sees only IP and port.

slides.title: Sticky sessions: quick relief, lasting trouble
slides.tldr: Sticky sessions always send the same user to the same server. That unbalances the load and loses the session when a server dies. The real fix is to keep sessions outside the server.

blocks.title: Always the same waiter
blocks.body: A family walks in and the manager says, "They always sit at Ryan's table", because only Ryan's notebook has their order. When 500 people from one big office arrive together, they all land on Ryan while the other waiters stand idle. If Ryan falls ill, the order notebook is lost with him.

marks.tip: Behind an office or mobile carrier NAT, thousands of users arrive with the same IP. They all land on one server.

blocks.caption: Open connections on the three servers after ip_hash is switched on (at the same moment)

items.label: Server 1 (office NAT)
items.tip: The 500 people of one company come from a single IP, and all of them are stuck on this one server.

items.label: Server 2
items.tip: Almost empty. Capacity is going to waste.

items.label: Server 3
items.tip: Nearly empty too, while server 1 is about to collapse.

blocks.code:
framework:
    session:
        # the session lives in Redis, so any server can read it
        handler_id: 'redis://redis.internal:6379'
        cookie_secure: auto
        cookie_samesite: lax

marks.tip: Every server now looks up the session in the same Redis. A server dying loses nobody's login, and ip_hash can go, replaced by least_conn.

blocks.body: Sticky sessions hide the symptom and leave the disease. The disease is state kept inside the server.

items: When a server dies or is deployed, all its users lose their session.
The price of the fix: one extra network call per request, and Redis itself becomes a SPOF, so give it a replica.
With autoscaling, new servers join but the existing users stay stuck on the old ones, so the new servers sit almost idle.
If you can't move the state right now, stick by cookie, not IP (free nginx: `hash $cookie_PHPSESSID consistent;`), and only temporarily. Put moving the session on your to-do list.

items.label: How to move sessions to Redis

check.q: Why can sticky sessions with ip_hash overload one server?
check.a: Many users behind an office or carrier NAT arrive with the same IP, and ip_hash always sends that IP to the same server.

slides.title: Add a node and the whole cache vanishes
slides.tldr: Split keys across nodes with `hash(key) % N` and changing N moves almost every key. Going from 4 to 5 nodes makes 80% of the cache miss at once.

blocks.title: Shelving books in a library
blocks.body: A library has 4 shelves and one rule: divide the book's number by 4, and the remainder tells you the shelf. The crowd grows, so a 5th shelf goes in and the rule becomes "divide by 5". Now about 80 out of every 100 books sit on the wrong shelf, and nobody can find anything. A cache cluster behaves exactly the same way.

marks.tip: As soon as count($this->nodes) changes, the result changes for nearly every key. Going from 4 to 5 nodes sends 80% of keys to a different node.

blocks.caption: Share of keys that change node when going from 4 to 5 nodes

items.label: hash % N
items.tip: Of every 20 keys only 4 stay on their old node. All the rest miss, and everyone rushes to the database at once.

items.label: Consistent hashing
items.tip: The new node takes only its own share (1/5). The other 80% of keys stay where they were.

blocks.body: When you add or remove cache nodes, you must not move every key. Only the part that has to move should move.

aside.title: The scale-out the night before a sale
aside.body: To prepare for the crowd, a team added one Redis node to their 4. Within a minute the hit rate fell from 95% to 20%, and the database went from 5 misses in every 100 requests to 80, sixteen times the queries, and slowed to a crawl. The move meant to ease the load made it worse.

items.label: What happens when everything misses at once

check.q: With hash % N over a 4-node cache, what happens when you add a fifth node?
check.a: About 80% of keys change node, so they all miss at once. The extra load lands on the database.

slides.title: Put them on a circle: the first node clockwise
slides.tldr: Hash both nodes and keys onto a circle. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Add or remove a node and only its neighbor's share moves.

blocks.title: Four coffee trucks around a traffic circle
blocks.body: Four coffee trucks park spaced out around a traffic circle. Wherever you stand, you walk clockwise and buy from the first truck you reach. If one truck drives away, its customers walk on to the next truck, and nobody else is affected.

blocks.caption: The circle runs 0-99. Nodes: A=10, B=40, C=70, D=90

rows.tip: Walking on from 25, the first node is B at 40, so cart:17 goes to B.
From 62 you reach C at 70.
There is no node after 95, so you wrap around past 0 and find A at 10. This is the wrap-around.
From 5 the first node is A at 10. In other words, A is responsible for the stretch from 91 to 10.

blocks.caption: What moves when nodes change

steps.title: 1. Node B leaves
steps.body: Keys that were in 11-40 go to C
steps.tip: Only B's own keys move. The keys of A, C and D stay where they were.

steps.title: 2. New node E=55 joins
steps.body: E takes the 41-55 part of C's range
steps.tip: E takes a slice only from the node right after it (C). The other nodes never notice.

steps.title: 3. Total movement
steps.body: On average about 1/N of the keys
steps.tip: When one node joins or leaves among N, roughly 1/N of all keys move. That is far less than the 80% of hash % N.

items.meaning: A function that turns any key, like cart:17, into a number. The same key always gives the same number.
Treating the whole hash range (say 0 to 2^32) as a circle, where the end connects back to the start.
Reaching the end of the circle and carrying on from the node at the start.

aside.body: Place the key, walk clockwise, the first node is the owner.

check.q: If node C (70) leaves the ring, where do the keys in 41-70 go, and does anything of A's move?
check.a: They go to the next node clockwise, D (90). A's keys don't move, because none of them were under C's responsibility.

slides.title: A small hash ring in PHP
slides.tldr: A ring is a sorted list of hashes plus a binary search. Give each node 150 virtual positions, then add a 5th node and measure how much moved.

blocks.body: The inner workings are small. Hash each node many times as `node#i` and keep the results in a sorted list. When a key arrives, hash it and binary-search that list for the first position that's larger. If you run off the end of the list, go back to the start. `remove()` just deletes that node's positions, and every other key keeps its owner.

marks.tip: 150 virtual positions per node. Too few and the split is uneven; too many and memory use grows and add() gets slower.
A bigger machine gets a bigger weight, so it gets more positions and a bigger share. add('big-1', 2) means twice as many.
Each position is tied to the name of the real node. The positions of one node end up scattered around the circle.
Drops only this node's positions. array_filter keeps the order, so no re-sort is needed, and every other key keeps its owner.
% count(...) is the wrap-around: when h is larger than every position, $lo reaches the end, and the % turns it into 0 so you return to the first position.

items: Don't write this yourself in production. Use the memcached client's ketama mode, nginx's `hash ... consistent`, or Redis Cluster. The code above is here so you can see how it works.
crc32 is small and fast, so it's fine for learning. Larger systems pick MurmurHash or xxHash for a better spread.
Every client must use the same hash function, the same node names and the same vnode count. Otherwise two clients look for the same key on two different nodes.

check.q: Why is `$lo % count($this->positions)` needed in nodeFor()?
check.a: If the key's hash is larger than every position, the first node clockwise is the very first position on the circle. The % performs that wrap-around.

slides.title: Virtual nodes: making every share equal
slides.tldr: With a single position per node, the shares come out badly uneven. Give each node many virtual positions and the shares even out, and a dead node's share spreads across everyone.

blocks.title: Scatter the kiosks
blocks.body: If 3 coffee trucks each park at one spot on the traffic circle, a big gap between two of them gives one truck far more customers. The fix: each owner puts out 150 small kiosks all around the circle. Now wherever you stand, there is a kiosk from every owner nearby, and the shares come out almost equal.

blocks.caption: Shares of three nodes (example numbers): 1 position vs 150

items.label: A: 1 position
items.tip: By luck it landed next to a big gap, so more than half of all keys fall on it.

items.label: B: 1 position
items.tip: A middling share. Still not equal.

items.label: C: 1 position
items.tip: Stuck in a small gap, it sits almost idle.

items.label: A: 150 positions
items.tip: Many small slices add up, and the share comes out almost equal.

items.label: B: 150 positions
items.tip: Almost exactly a third, as it should be.

items.label: C: 150 positions
items.tip: More positions means the law of averages evens out the share.

blocks.title: What else virtual nodes give you
items: When a node dies, its keys spread over all the nodes instead of landing on a single neighbor.
Give a bigger machine more vnodes and it takes a bigger share, like a weight.
The cost: a little more memory and a little more time to add or remove.
When a node dies you lose the cache for its keys. They will all go to the database together, so have something in place to stop a stampede.

aside.body: One node, many positions: the shares come out equal, and everyone shares the pain.

items.label: Handling the storm of misses when a node dies

check.q: Without vnodes, with just 1 position per node, what is the problem?
check.a: The shares are uneven: one node gets a big gap and carries too much, another sits almost idle. And when a node dies, its whole load falls on a single neighbor.

slides.title: Where you meet it in the real world
slides.tldr: Cache clusters, nginx upstreams and partitioned stores like Cassandra and the Dynamo design use consistent hashing. Redis Cluster is close but different: 16384 fixed hash slots.

blocks.caption: Where it is used and how

cells: Less cache lost when nodes are added
rows.tip: The client runs the ring itself; the server nodes don't know about each other.

cells: The same URL goes to the same cache server
rows.tip: To keep each server's cache separate, the same request has to go to the same server.

cells: A hash ring over the partition key
Data is split and replicated across many nodes
rows.tip: Here the ring decides where the actual data is stored, not just a cache.

cells: Slots can be moved, instead of a ring
rows.tip: The slot is CRC16(key) % 16384, and each slot belongs to one node. When nodes change, whole slots move.

marks.tip: Without `consistent` this is plain hash % N. One word in a short line, yet it saves your whole cache after a scale-out.

blocks.title: What consistent hashing does not do
items: Hot keys: one famous key still lives on a single node (fix below).
Moving data: for permanent data, the data really has to be copied to the new node (rebalancing).
Replication: keeping several copies of a key is a separate job; the ring only names the first node.

marks.tip: product:iphone#0 to #7 land on up to 8 different nodes, so the reads are shared out instead of hitting one.
The price: 8 writes per update, and for a moment the copies can disagree. Use it for the few hot keys only.

use: Caches or partitioned stores where nodes come and go
When the same key must always go to the same server (cache affinity)
avoid: A small fixed cluster whose nodes never change
You have just one Redis node

check.q: One viral product key is being read more than any other across the site. Will consistent hashing ease the load on its node?
check.a: No. It is a single key, so the ring keeps it on one node. A hot key needs a different tactic, such as a small local cache inside the app, or several copies of the key.

slides.title: Two servers, both thinking "I'm the leader"
slides.tldr: When only one of many servers should do a job, you have to pick a leader. If the network stalls, both can believe they're the leader, and the job runs twice.

blocks.title: A school with two principals
blocks.body: When the principal goes on leave, the vice principal is supposed to take charge. But the vice principal's phone was off, so she never learned that the principal had come back. Both of them ran the monthly payroll, and some teachers were paid twice.

blocks.caption: A payroll cron on two servers: both believed they were the leader

actors.label: Server A
actors.tip: It was the leader before. Now it is stuck for a while on the network, or in a GC pause (the program freezes while it cleans up its memory).

actors.label: Server B
actors.tip: Hearing nothing from A, it concluded that A had died.

actors.label: Payroll table
actors.tip: The database won't object by itself, whoever writes.

messages.label: I'm the leader: paying May's salaries
A is silent. I'm the leader, paying salaries
messages.tip: B has no way of knowing that A isn't dead, only stuck.

messages.label: Back, and paying the rest too

messages.tip: Each of them had a reason to think it was the leader. This is exactly split brain.

blocks.body: On many servers, "only one does it" means someone becomes leader by agreement of the majority.

aside.body: From the outside you can't tell whether a server has died or is just slow. So B deciding alone that "A is dead" is dangerous. This segment teaches how to decide together.

items.meaning: A rule for choosing one server out of many, and choosing a new one when the leader dies.
When the network splits in two and both halves think they're the leader.

check.q: Why can't B be sure that A has died?
check.a: From the outside, a dead server looks the same as a slow one or one stuck on the network. Getting no reply doesn't mean "dead".

slides.title: Quorum: decisions pass by majority
slides.tldr: A quorum is a majority (N/2 + 1). That many members must agree for a decision to pass. If the network splits in two, only one side can hold a majority.

blocks.title: A five-member city council
blocks.body: A city council has 5 members, and a ruling needs at least 3 to agree. Snow blocks the road and the council splits into a group of 3 and a group of 2. What happens? The group of 3 can issue a ruling and the group of 2 can't. So the two groups can never hand down opposite rulings.

blocks.caption: How many nodes can die while the system keeps working

rows.tip: With a single node, its death stops everything. That is a SPOF (single point of failure): one thing breaks and all of it stops.
The smallest realistic cluster. Even if one dies, the other two still make a majority.
One more than 3 nodes, but the same fault tolerance (1). The extra node only adds cost.
Very common in production. Even with two dead, the remaining three can still decide.
More nodes means every decision talks to more members, so it is slower. That is why you rarely go beyond 7.

blocks.body: Quorum = N/2 + 1. Keep the number of nodes odd: an even number is extra cost, not extra tolerance.

aside.body: Two halves can't both be a majority. All of consensus stands on that one fact.

items: Put the nodes in different racks or availability zones, so that a single incident can't take out the majority.
The price: if the cluster loses its majority, it stops accepting writes rather than risk two leaders. It picks safety over staying up.

check.q: A 5-node cluster splits into 3 and 2 by a network fault. Which side can accept writes?
check.a: The side with 3 nodes, because it holds a majority (quorum = 3). The 2-node side can't make any new decisions.

slides.title: Raft: choosing a leader and matching the log
slides.tldr: In Raft one leader takes all writes and sends them to followers, and a write is final only once a majority has it. If the leader goes quiet, a vote picks a new one.

blocks.title: The chair of the council
blocks.body: The chair regularly tells everyone, "I'm here." When nothing has been heard for a while, the member who loses patience first says, "We need a new chair, vote for me." With 3 votes, that member becomes chair. The chair writes the ruling and sends it around, and once 3 members accept it, the ruling is final.

blocks.caption: The core cycle of Raft

steps.title: 1. Everyone is a follower
steps.body: Stay quiet while the leader's heartbeats arrive
steps.tip: The leader keeps sending small messages (heartbeats) to say it is alive.

steps.title: 2. Timeout, candidate
steps.body: No heartbeat: raise the term and ask for votes
steps.tip: Each member has a different timeout (say a random 150-300ms), so they don't all become candidates together.

steps.title: 3. Majority vote, leader
steps.body: With a quorum, it becomes the new leader
steps.tip: In each term a member casts just one vote. So two leaders can't be elected in the same term.

steps.title: 4. It sends the log
steps.body: The leader sends each write to the followers
steps.tip: All writes pile up in one ordered log. Matching that log is the real work of consensus.

steps.title: 5. Final once a majority agrees
steps.body: When a quorum acks, the write is committed
steps.tip: A committed write is never lost, even if the leader dies. A new leader can only come from members who know about it.

blocks.title: Don't write it yourself, use it
items: etcd (Raft): all of Kubernetes' state lives here.
ZooKeeper (Zab, close to Paxos): older Kafka versions, Hadoop. Consul uses Raft too.
Paxos came before Raft with the same guarantees, but it is far harder to understand and to build.

items.meaning: The number of an election round; it goes up with each new election. Nobody obeys a leader from an old term.
Written to a majority of nodes, so it can't be lost any more.

use: Small but critical data: config, who the leader is, locks (through etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul)
avoid: Big data or heavy write rates: every write waits for a majority, and one leader takes them all
Writing Raft yourself: there are too many subtle bugs, so use a ready-made service

check.q: Why can't two leaders exist in the same term in Raft?
check.a: Each member votes only once per term, and becoming leader takes a majority of votes. Two different majorities can't both give the same votes.

slides.title: "Only one runs it" with Symfony Lock
slides.tldr: For ordinary cases, give a job to one runner at a time with Symfony Lock's LockFactory. Set a short TTL, call refresh() during long jobs, and release() at the end.

blocks.body: Back to the payroll cron. Take a named lock for each month's job: if you get it, do the work, and if you don't, return. Change the DSN and the same code runs on a Redis, PostgreSQL or ZooKeeper lock.

blocks.code:
framework:
    lock: '%env(LOCK_DSN)%'
    # LOCK_DSN=redis://redis:6379
    # LOCK_DSN=postgresql+advisory://app:secret@db/shop
    # LOCK_DSN=zookeeper://zk1:2181,zk2:2181,zk3:2181

marks.tip: A single DSN decides the store. You can move away from Redis without changing the code.
Thanks to the ttl, even if the server dies mid-job, the lock frees itself after 60 seconds. Leave it out and Symfony uses 300 seconds, so a crash would block payroll for 5 minutes.
It extends the lease on every step. But this alone is not safety: after a pause you can still lose the lock (next slide).

items: This lock is for the "don't run the job twice" kind of benefit. Where a mistake costs money or stock, don't rely on a lock alone.
Keep the payment idempotent per employee: a unique constraint on (employee_id, month) means a second payment is impossible even if the lock slips.

items.label: Kinds of locks and how to use them

check.q: What goes wrong if the lock's ttl is far too long, or shorter than the job?
check.a: Too long: if the server dies, nobody can take the job until the ttl runs out. Too short: the lock expires mid-job and a second server starts. So use a short ttl and call refresh() while the work runs.

slides.title: When a lock expires: the fencing token
slides.tldr: If the lock holder pauses or slows down, the lock expires and someone else gets it, yet the first process wakes up and keeps writing. The fix is a fencing token: the storage itself rejects the stale token.

blocks.title: Walking up with an old token
