blocks.body: At a bank you take token number 33 and go to get a drink of water. By the time you're back, number 34 has been called. The clerk looks at your 33 and says, "That token is canceled." You yourself don't know your turn has passed, so canceling it is the counter's job.

blocks.caption: The database stops the slowed-down A

actors.label: Lock service
actors.tip: With every lock it grants, it hands out an ever-increasing token.

actors.label: Worker A
actors.tip: It gets the lock first, then freezes in a 40-second pause.

actors.label: Worker B
actors.tip: It gets the lock after A's lease has expired.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: It checks the token on every write and honors only the newest.

messages.note: GC pause for 40 seconds, lease expires

messages.label: Write (token 33)
messages.tip: A still thinks the lock is its own.
The last line of defense is the database, not the lock service. It recognizes the stale token.

blocks.code:
-- taking the lock and bumping the token in one atomic step
UPDATE job_locks
   SET holder = :me, token = token + 1, expires_at = now() + interval '30 seconds'
 WHERE name = 'payroll' AND expires_at < now()
RETURNING token;

-- check the token on every write
UPDATE payroll_runs
   SET status = 'paid', last_token = :token
 WHERE id = :run AND last_token <= :token;
-- 0 rows affected means you are a stale leader: stop

marks.tip: The token increases together with the lock grant. If you fetch it from a sequence after getting the lock, a pause in between can put things in the wrong order.
<= because the same leader can write several times with the same token. When a lower token arrives, no row is updated.

blocks.body: A lock expires, and its holder doesn't know it. So the last line of defense is the storage, not the lock holder.

items: A single Redis lock can be lost on failover: if the primary dies before the write reaches the replica, the new primary doesn't know the lock.
etcd's revision, ZooKeeper's zxid and sequence nodes naturally give an increasing token; the storage still has to check it.
Symfony Lock hands out no token. For fencing, keep a counter in your own table as above, or take etcd's revision.

use: If doing the job twice only costs a little: a plain Symfony Lock is enough
avoid: If money or stock changes: don't trust a lock alone without a fencing token or idempotency
If the target is an outside service that can't check a token (email, payments): use an idempotency key instead

items.label: Why you can't trust a clock to time out a lease

check.q: Why can't the lock holder itself be sure its lock is still valid?
check.a: While it was paused or stuck on the network it was asleep, and the lease expired and someone else got the lock. On waking it has no way to tell, which is why the storage must check the token.

slides.title: I placed an order, but "no such order"
slides.tldr: A replica gets the primary's data a little late. During that gap a user can't see their own write, data can jump backwards in time, or events can show up in the wrong order.

blocks.title: The main post office and the local branch
blocks.body: Ryan deposits a money order at the main post office, and it's written in their ledger. A mail carrier needs a few minutes to carry that line to the branch's ledger. If Ryan walks straight into the branch and asks, he hears, "There's no such record." The post office made no mistake; the copy just hasn't arrived yet.

blocks.caption: Write goes to the primary, read comes from the replica: a wrong answer in the 2 seconds between

actors.label: Ryan
actors.tip: He places an order and immediately wants to see the result page.

actors.label: App
actors.tip: It sends the write to the primary, and the read that shows the page to the replica.

actors.label: Replica
actors.tip: A copy of the primary. A write reaches it with a small delay.

messages.note: The copy hasn't arrived yet (lag 2 seconds)

messages.label: 404: where is my order?
messages.tip: The user thinks the money was taken and the order lost. In fact the data is fine; it was just read from the wrong place.

blocks.title: Three kinds of trouble from lag
items: Not seeing your own write: you place an order and it says "no such order".
Time going backwards: you see the new data once, then refresh and see the old (on another replica).
Order reversed: the answer shows up, but the question it answers hasn't arrived yet.

aside.body: Read replicas spread the read load, but the price is losing the "always the latest" guarantee. This step is about deciding where you can live with that and where you can't.

check.q: Right after placing an order, the page said "no such order" and then was fine a moment later. What is the most likely cause?
check.a: Replication lag. The order was written to the primary, but the read for the page went to a replica that hadn't received the write yet.

slides.title: Show users their own writes
slides.tldr: For a few seconds after a write, serve that user's reads from the primary. Everyone else reads from a replica. Critical reads (money, stock) always go to the primary.

blocks.body: The simple rule: a user who has just written gets their reads from the primary for a few seconds. Lag usually stays within a few seconds, so 5 seconds of primary reads is enough to keep them from seeing stale data. Below, a small cookie is set after a write, and reads check it to choose the connection.

marks.tip: DoctrineBundle autowires the connection named "replica" as `$replicaConnection`. The default connection comes in by type alone.
After any POST, PUT or DELETE a cookie with the time is set in the user's browser. The server keeps no state.
Within 5 seconds of the last write, read from the primary. Once more than the lag has passed, the replica is safe.

blocks.title: Other ways
items: Return the new order in the POST response itself, so the page doesn't need a read at all.
Always read critical things like money, stock or permissions from the primary.
Pin each user to one replica (code below), so time never goes backwards.

marks.tip: The price: if that replica dies, its users move to another one and may see an older copy once. Load can also be uneven between replicas.

items: Measure lag: on a PostgreSQL replica, `SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp();`. Keep an alert on it at all times.
Keep the sticky window longer than the p99 of the lag, or gaps will remain.

use: Right after a user's own write: a post, an edit, an order
Everything else may read a replica: feeds, counts, lists that can be a few seconds old
avoid: Money, stock, permissions: always read the primary, not just for 5 seconds
If lag often runs past 5 seconds: fix the lag first, the window can't cover it

items.desc: run on the replica: how far behind it is
run on the primary: the lag of each replica

check.q: A user refreshes the feed 3 seconds after posting. Why do you read from the primary, and for how long?
check.a: The post may not have reached the replica yet. So after a user's last write, serve their reads from the primary for longer than the lag (say 5 seconds).

slides.title: Moving the warehouse while the shop stays open
slides.tldr: Big data can't be moved in one night. Build the new place, write new data to both, copy the old data, verify, then move reads over step by step.

blocks.title: Changing warehouses with the shop open
blocks.body: The old warehouse has become too small and the stock must go to a new one. But the shop can't close for even a day. So new stock goes into both warehouses, trucks carry the old stock over bit by bit, and then the books are checked. Only when everything matches do customers get sent to the new warehouse.

blocks.caption: The plan for moving big data, the same for a new database, a new shard or a new table

steps.title: 1. Build the new place
steps.body: An empty schema, indexes ready
steps.tip: The new table, shard or database is ready in advance. Nothing has changed in the old system yet.

steps.title: 2. Turn on dual write
steps.body: New writes go to both old and new
steps.tip: From this step on, new data no longer falls behind. Write it as an upsert, so a change to a row the backfill hasn't copied yet still lands.

steps.title: 3. Backfill
steps.body: Copy old data slowly, in small batches
steps.tip: It runs slowly so the live site isn't put under pressure. The next slide has the code.

steps.title: 4. Verify
steps.body: Match counts and checksums, shadow read
steps.tip: A shadow read means reading from the new place too and comparing the results, while the user still sees the old one.

steps.title: 5. Move reads
steps.body: 1% → 10% → 100% from the new place
steps.tip: Moving in steps means that if a problem shows up, few users suffer, and you can step back one stage.

steps.title: 6. Retire the old one
steps.body: Stop writes, keep it a while, then delete
steps.tip: Don't delete straight away. Keeping the old one for a while gives you a way back if a mistake turns up.

blocks.body: Big data doesn't move in one jolt. Move in small steps, check at every step, and keep the way back open.

use: Changing the database or storage engine
Rebalancing after adding or removing shards
Changing the structure of a big table
avoid: A small table that copies in a minute: the simple way is enough
When a short planned downtime is fine: dual write doubles the writes and adds code you must remove later

items.label: Moving less data when a shard is added

check.q: Before moving reads to the new place, which must start first, dual write or backfill, and why?
check.a: Dual write. Otherwise new writes that arrive while the backfill runs never reach the new place, and that gap never gets filled.

slides.title: Backfill: small batches, slow pace, stop and resume
slides.tldr: Run a backfill in small batches by id (keyset), with idempotent INSERTs, and pause when replica lag grows. The live site stays fast, and a stopped job can be resumed.

blocks.code:
INSERT INTO orders_v2 (id, status, total_cents)
SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM orders;

marks.tip: Tens of millions of rows in one transaction: long locks, a surge of WAL (the log of every change that replicas replay), replica lag for minutes on end. If it fails halfway, everything rolls back.
Keyset with id > ?, not OFFSET. Every batch is equally fast, even at the 10-millionth row.
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes it idempotent: rerunning is harmless, and a row dual write already put in the new table, with a newer value, isn't overwritten by this older copy.
If replica lag is over 5 seconds, pause for 5 seconds, otherwise 0.2. That way reads on the live site don't slow down either.

items: Keep each batch a small transaction (about 1000 rows). Bigger ones increase locks and lag.
Slow is fine: 10 million rows at 1,000 per batch with 0.2s pauses is 10,000 batches, about 33 minutes of pauses plus the copying. One quiet night is enough.
Run it in the quiet of the night, and make the batch size and pause options of the command so you can change them while it runs.

items.desc: after a stop, from the last id

check.q: The backfill command crashed at midnight. Why is rerunning it harmless, and where do you restart?
check.a: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is idempotent, so rows that were already copied aren't inserted a second time. Restart with `--from` set to the last logged id.

slides.title: When dual write slips: the old one is the truth, so verify
slides.tldr: Writing to two places, one can fail. Treat the old system as the source of truth, repair failed writes to the new one later, and verify step by step with counts and checksums.

blocks.body: In a dual write the two writes are separate, so one can succeed while the other fails. A failure on the new side must not block the user's order. So the old one is the source of truth, and when the new one fails you log it and queue a repair job.

marks.tip: Until reads move over, the truth is the old one. If it fails here, the whole save fails, which is the normal behavior.
RepairOrderCopy reads the row from the old store again and puts it in the new one. It must be idempotent, because it may run more than once.

blocks.file: The same checksum on both sides (by id range)
blocks.code:
SELECT count(*) AS n,
       sum(hashtextextended(concat_ws('|', id, status, total_cents), 0)) AS checksum
  FROM orders            -- on the new side, run it against orders_v2
 WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 100000;

marks.tip: Matching counts isn't enough. With the same number of rows, some values can still differ, and the checksum catches that.
Compare in id ranges, not the whole table at once. When there is a mismatch you know exactly which slice has the problem.

blocks.body: Don't move reads without verifying. Matching counts is not enough; the values must match.

items: If writes reach the old and new in different orders ("A then B" vs "B then A"), the final values can differ. Keep writes to the same row in order, through one queue.
Counts on live data never match exactly. Use a quiet night, or an older cutoff on updated_at.
If the process dies between the two writes, no repair job exists. Only the checksum run will catch that gap.

items.label: Reconciliation: matching two sets of books
A safe second write with an outbox

check.q: Both tables have 12,000,000 rows. Why is cutover still not safe?
check.a: A count only matches the number of rows, not their values. Some rows may differ in status or amount. Match the values with a checksum by range, or a shadow read.

slides.title: The branch phone line is cut: pay out or not?
slides.tldr: When the link between two copies of the data is cut, a system has to choose: answer even though it may be wrong, or refuse to answer until it is sure.

blocks.title: One account, the New York and Chicago branches
blocks.body: Ryan's account holds $500, and both the New York and Chicago branches know the balance. Then the phone line between the two branches goes down. Now Ryan is in New York and his wife is in Chicago, and both want to withdraw $400. Each branch has only two paths in front of it.

blocks.caption: With the line cut, both branches said "yes"

actors.label: Ryan (New York)
actors.tip: He has come to the New York branch to withdraw $400.

actors.label: New York branch
actors.tip: It sees a balance of $500 on its own books. It knows nothing about Chicago.

actors.label: Chicago branch
actors.tip: Its own books say $500 too. It knows nothing about New York.

actors.label: Wife (Chicago)
actors.tip: At the same moment she has come to Chicago to withdraw $400 from the same account.

messages.tip: Neither branch knows whether the other has died or only the line is cut.
Both got an answer (available), but the books no longer add up (inconsistent).

blocks.title: The two paths in front of a branch
items: Pay out: reconcile the books when the line is back (everyone gets an answer, but it may be wrong).
Refuse: wait until the line returns (the books stay right, but nobody gets served).

aside.body: Once the network splits, no system can give both the correct answer and an answer every time. If you don't decide this choice in advance, it gets decided at random in the middle of the crisis.

check.q: With the line cut, what is lost if both branches pay out, and what would be lost if they didn't?
check.a: If they pay, consistency (correct books) is lost. If they don't, availability (always getting an answer) is lost. You couldn't have saved both.

slides.title: CAP: splits will happen, so pick C or A
slides.tldr: You can't avoid network partitions. So CAP really says: during a partition you stay consistent (CP) or stay available (AP). It is a choice per feature, not a label for a database.

blocks.caption: Two paths during a partition

columns.title: CP: right answer or wait
items: Line cut: withdrawals stop
The minority side returns an error or times out
Balance, stock, seats, locks, leaders
etcd and ZooKeeper take this path
columns.tip: The path for features where no answer beats a wrong one. The majority side keeps going and the minority side stops.

columns.title: AP: always answer, reconcile later
items: Both sides answer
Some answers may be stale
Likes, feed, cart, view count
When the line is back, the changes are merged
columns.tip: The path for features that must always respond and can tolerate slightly stale data. You have to reconcile afterwards.

blocks.title: What a partition really is
items: Two nodes can't reach each other. A cut cable, a failed switch or a firewall mistake all count.
Slow means dead: in a 30-second GC pause, a node looks lost to the others once the timeout passes.
Rare, but real. A big system sees it at least a few times a year, so you can't design on the assumption that it won't happen.

blocks.body: CAP is not "pick two of three". Partitions will happen, and then you choose: the right answer (C) or an answer at all (A).

items.meaning: Every read sees the latest write, as if there were just one copy of the data. Not the same as the C in ACID (obeying the rules).
Every live node answers every request, instead of an error or waiting forever.
Messages between nodes getting lost or delayed.
A program freezing for a moment while it cleans up its memory. To the others it looks dead.

aside.body: With no partition, you have both C and A. When a partition comes, one must go.

check.q: "We chose a CA database, so we don't worry about partitions." What is wrong with that?
check.a: A partition isn't something you choose, it's something that happens. A system with several nodes can have its network split, and then it has to give up either C or A.

slides.title: PACELC: even with the line fine, you pay
slides.tldr: Even with no partition (Else), writing with everyone's agreement across places costs latency. PACELC says: in a partition, A or C; otherwise, L (latency) or C.

blocks.title: Phoning Chicago every single time
blocks.body: The line is fine. Before every withdrawal the New York branch could phone Chicago and reconcile the books: perfect, but it takes 1 minute. Or it could just pay out without asking: 10 seconds, but its view of Chicago may be slightly stale. Even with a healthy line, you pay this price.

blocks.caption: Approximate time of one write, by how many must agree

items.label: Write to one server
items.tip: Nobody else to talk to, so it is fast. But if the server dies, you can lose data.

items.label: Quorum across 3 AZs
items.tip: A majority of three data centers in the same city agree. A small delay for a lot of safety.

items.label: Quorum across 3 continents
items.tip: The speed-of-light limit: agreement from a distant region takes time, and every write pays this delay.

blocks.caption: Where each system leans (default configs; they can be changed)

rows.tip: It puts fast answers and staying up first. Reads may be slightly stale. Quorum reads can change that.
It always takes agreement from a majority, so writes take a bit longer, but answers are correct.
A commit waits until the sync replica confirms. Safe, but every write adds network delay.

cells: PostgreSQL + reading from an async replica
rows.tip: Fast reads, but replication lag means you may see stale data.

items.meaning: A majority of the copies, like 2 of 3. A write counts once a majority has it.
Availability zone: a separate data center in the same city, with its own power and network.
A copy that must confirm every write before the commit returns. Async copies catch up later.

aside.body: PACELC = If Partition then A or C; Else Latency or Consistency.

check.q: Why are writes slow when every one needs a majority across three continents, even when the network is healthy?
check.a: Agreement from a distant region takes time because of the speed of light. You are paying latency all the time to buy consistency, the "Else" part of PACELC.

slides.title: Choose CP or AP per feature in one app
slides.tldr: Not for the whole database but for each feature, ask: is wrong data worse, or no answer? Money and stock go CP; likes and feeds go AP.

blocks.caption: Which path for which feature, and what the user sees
headers: What they see in a partition

rows.tip: Money paid out against a wrong balance is hard to get back. So if you aren't sure, it's better not to do it.
The harm of selling one seat to two people is far bigger than a short wait.
A few likes off harms nobody; always answering is what matters.

cells: A slightly stale page from cache
rows.tip: Even a stale list beats no list. It corrects itself after a while.

cells: You can always add, and it is reconciled later
rows.tip: The famous Amazon Dynamo example: adding to the cart never fails, and the two copies are merged afterwards.

marks.tip: A money write always goes to the primary, never to some stale copy. The idempotency key means a retry after a lost reply can't pay out twice.
If it can't be sure, it returns 503 with Retry-After. The user is told to try later, and no wrong figure is produced.
A number up to 30 seconds old, on purpose. In return the nearby replica keeps answering even when the link to the primary is cut.
Browsers and the CDN can keep it for 30 seconds too, so the database is barely touched.

use: CP: a mistake costs money, stock or legal trouble
AP: stale data hurts nobody, and getting no answer is worse
avoid: AP for balances or seats
CP for feeds and likes

items: CP costs availability: during a split users see errors. Show a clear message, and make the retry safe with an idempotency key.

items.meaning: The HTTP status for "service unavailable right now, try again".
A response header telling the client how many seconds to wait before trying again.
A unique id sent with a request, so a repeat of it is recognized and not done twice.

items.label: What to show when a dependency breaks

check.q: Flight seat booking and "how many people liked this post": which is CP, which is AP, and why?
check.a: Seat booking is CP: selling one seat twice does big damage, so wait if you aren't sure. Likes are AP: a slightly stale number hurts nobody, and getting an answer every time matters.

slides.title: Choosing AP means owing a reconciliation
slides.tldr: In AP, both sides change the same data separately. "Last write wins" depends on clocks and silently drops one change. You need a merge rule built in advance.

blocks.caption: Two ways to reconcile when the cart changed on both sides

columns.title: Last write wins
items: Shoes added to the cart in New York
A watch added in Chicago at the same time
Whoever's clock runs further ahead wins
The other is lost, and nobody knows
columns.tip: It keeps the write with the latest timestamp and throws the rest away. Simple, but it quietly loses data.

columns.title: Merge
items: The shoes and the watch both stay
If the same product is on both sides, keep the larger quantity
The rule is decided per feature
When it gets complex, use a CRDT
columns.tip: It takes both sides' changes and builds one result. No data is lost, but you have to design the rule for each feature.

marks.tip: client_ts is the clock on the user's phone. If that clock runs a few minutes ahead, it wins forever, and other people's newer changes can't get in.
For the same sku on both sides, keep the larger quantity. The rule changes from feature to feature.
Without these tombstones a deleted item comes back, as it did in Dynamo's cart. The price: remove beats add, so a re-added item needs a new line id.

blocks.body: AP means "we'll reconcile later". With no reconciliation rule, it isn't AP, it's silently losing data.

items: Server clocks aren't exact either; use a clock for LWW and even a small skew loses changes.
After picking AP, if you bolt on outside actions like refunds or emails, those can happen twice too, so keep them idempotent.

items.meaning: Last write wins: when two copies disagree, keep the one with the newest timestamp.
A data type built so that copies changed separately always merge to the same result.
A marker that says "this was deleted", so a merge doesn't bring the item back.

items.label: Why you can't order events by clock
Keeping events in the right order

check.q: When is the "last write wins" rule dangerous in an AP system, and what is the alternative?
check.a: When both sides change something at the same time, one is lost silently, and clock skew can make the wrong side win. The alternative: a per-feature merge rule, or a CRDT.
